| **ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Deep Dive** | Lecture + Case Study | The international gold standard for ISMS certification. Structure: clauses 4–10 define ISMS requirements (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement). Annex A contains 93 controls organized into 4 themes (Organizational, People, Physical, Technological) - reduced from 114 controls in 14 domains in the 2013 version. Certification process: Stage 1 (documentation review), Stage 2 (implementation audit), surveillance audits (annual), recertification (every 3 years). Real-world case study: after the 2017 NotPetya attack cost Maersk an estimated $300 million, the company rebuilt its security program using ISO 27001 as the foundation, achieving certification across its global operations within two years. The certification provided a structured framework for recovery and demonstrated to customers and partners that Maersk had fundamentally improved its security posture. |
| **NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0** | Lecture + Diagram | Updated in February 2024, NIST CSF 2.0 adds a sixth core function - Govern - to the original five (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover). This addition reflects ISACA's own emphasis on governance. Implementation Tiers (1–4) describe the degree of rigor in cybersecurity risk management practices. Profiles allow organizations to describe their current and target cybersecurity posture. Real-world adoption: the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) Cybersecurity Framework draws heavily from NIST CSF, requiring all financial institutions in the Kingdom to implement controls aligned with its structure. Discuss how NIST CSF 2.0's Govern function overlaps with CISM Domain 1. |
| **CIS Controls v8** | Lecture | The Center for Internet Security (CIS) Controls provide a prioritized, actionable set of 18 control categories. Implementation Groups (IGs) allow organizations to adopt controls progressively: IG1 (essential cyber hygiene, 56 safeguards - suitable for small organizations), IG2 (additional safeguards for organizations with IT staff, 130 total), IG3 (comprehensive, 153 total - for organizations with dedicated security teams). Real-world example: the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) recommends CIS Controls as the baseline for US state and local government cybersecurity programs. Discuss how CIS Controls complement rather than replace frameworks like NIST CSF and ISO 27001. |
| **Framework Comparison & Selection** | Interactive Discussion | Present a comparison matrix across dimensions: scope, approach, certification available, regulatory recognition, complexity, and best-fit scenarios. Key insight: frameworks are not mutually exclusive. A common pattern is ISO 27001 for ISMS structure and certification, NIST CSF for risk-based prioritization, CIS Controls for tactical implementation guidance, and COBIT for IT governance alignment. Students discuss which framework(s) they would recommend for three scenarios: (1) a 50-person startup seeking SOC 2 certification, (2) a government agency in the UAE, (3) a multinational bank operating across 15 countries. |
| **The Policy Hierarchy** | Lecture + Diagram | Define the four levels. Policy: high-level statement of management intent and direction (e.g., "All sensitive data must be encrypted"). Standard: mandatory requirements that support the policy (e.g., "Encryption must use AES-256 or equivalent"). Procedure: step-by-step instructions for implementing the standard (e.g., "To enable BitLocker on a Windows endpoint, follow these steps..."). Guideline: recommended practices that are not mandatory (e.g., "Consider using a password manager to generate unique passwords"). Discuss the relationship between levels: policies are approved by senior management, standards by the CISO, procedures by the security operations team, and guidelines by subject matter experts. |
| **Developing Effective Security Policies** | Lecture + Template | A good security policy includes: purpose (why the policy exists), scope (who and what it applies to), policy statements (the actual requirements), roles and responsibilities, compliance requirements, enforcement mechanisms (consequences of non-compliance), exceptions process, and review schedule. Real-world example: the SANS Institute publishes a library of policy templates that many organizations use as starting points. Discuss common policy types: acceptable use, access control, data classification, incident response, remote work, BYOD, encryption, third-party security, and data retention. Walk through a sample acceptable use policy. |
| **Policy Lifecycle Management** | Lecture | Policies are living documents. Lifecycle stages: (1) Development - drafted by the security team with input from stakeholders. (2) Review - reviewed by legal, HR, IT, and affected business units. (3) Approval - approved by the appropriate authority (CISO, executive committee, or board depending on scope). (4) Communication - distributed to all affected parties with training and acknowledgment. (5) Enforcement - monitored through technical controls, audits, and management oversight. (6) Review - reassessed annually or when triggered by significant changes (new regulations, incidents, organizational changes). (7) Retirement - formally withdrawn when no longer applicable. Real-world failure: the Target breach (2013) revealed that the company had a security policy requiring network segmentation between its corporate and POS networks, but the policy had never been implemented or enforced. The policy existed; the controls did not. |
| **Security Program Metrics & KPIs** | Lecture + Examples | Metrics must be meaningful, measurable, and actionable. Categories: Operational metrics (mean time to detect/respond, patch compliance rate, vulnerability remediation SLA adherence). Compliance metrics (audit findings open/closed, policy exception count, training completion rate). Risk metrics (number of high/critical risks, risk treatment progress, KRI status). Program maturity metrics (maturity level by framework domain, year-over-year improvement). Real-world example: JPMorgan Chase reportedly tracks over 200 security metrics, but presents only 12 key indicators to the board - a curated dashboard that tells the story without overwhelming the audience. Discuss the danger of vanity metrics (metrics that look good but do not drive decisions). |
| **Session Summary & Preview** | Wrap-up | Recap frameworks (COBIT, ISO 27001, NIST CSF, CIS Controls), policy hierarchy, policy lifecycle, and program metrics. Preview Session 8: Control Design, Selection & Implementation - moving from policy to practice, translating requirements into operational controls. |

---

## Key Concepts & Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **COBIT 2019** | ISACA's framework for governance and management of enterprise information and technology, featuring 40 objectives across 5 domains and design factors for organizational tailoring. |
| **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** | The international standard for information security management systems, requiring organizations to establish, implement, maintain, and continually improve an ISMS. Annex A contains 93 controls across 4 themes. |
| **NIST CSF 2.0** | The updated NIST Cybersecurity Framework (February 2024) with six core functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. Includes implementation tiers and organizational profiles. |
| **CIS Controls v8** | A prioritized set of 18 control categories with 153 safeguards, organized into three Implementation Groups (IG1, IG2, IG3) for progressive adoption based on organizational resources. |
| **Policy** | A high-level statement of management intent and direction that establishes expectations for behavior and decision-making across the organization. |
| **Standard** | A mandatory requirement that supports a policy by specifying the minimum level of performance or configuration required. |
| **Procedure** | A detailed, step-by-step set of instructions for performing a specific task or process in compliance with a standard. |
| **Guideline** | A recommended practice or approach that supports a policy or standard but is not mandatory. Provides flexibility for implementation. |
| **Statement of Applicability (SoA)** | An ISO 27001 requirement that documents which Annex A controls are applicable to the organization, which are implemented, and the justification for any exclusions. |
| **Maturity Model** | A framework for assessing the sophistication and effectiveness of an organization's processes, typically using a scale from Level 1 (Initial/Ad Hoc) to Level 5 (Optimized/Continuous Improvement). |
| **Vanity Metric** | A measurement that appears impressive but does not provide actionable insight or drive meaningful decision-making. Example: "We blocked 10 million attacks this month" without context on what constitutes an "attack." |

---

## Real-World Examples & Scenarios

**Scenario 1 - Maersk's Post-NotPetya Rebuild (Framework Implementation)**
On June 27, 2017, the NotPetya malware struck Maersk, the world's largest container shipping company. Within hours, 49,000 laptops, 3,500 servers, and the entire Active Directory infrastructure were destroyed. The company was forced to reinstall its entire IT infrastructure - 45,000 PCs and 4,000 servers - in just 10 days. The estimated cost exceeded $300 million. In the aftermath, Maersk's leadership made a strategic decision: rather than simply rebuilding what existed before, they would build a fundamentally stronger security program. They selected ISO 27001 as the framework for their new ISMS, supplemented by NIST CSF for risk-based prioritization. The certification process forced the company to document every process, classify every asset, and implement controls systematically rather than reactively. Within two years, Maersk achieved ISO 27001 certification across its global operations. The framework provided not just security improvement but a structured recovery methodology and a credible signal to customers that the company had learned from the incident.

**Scenario 2 - Target's Policy-Implementation Gap (Policy Lifecycle Failure)**
The 2013 Target breach, which exposed 40 million credit card numbers and 70 million customer records, revealed a critical gap between policy and implementation. Target's security policies required network segmentation between its corporate network and its point-of-sale (POS) systems. The policy existed. The standard existed. But the controls were never fully implemented - the HVAC vendor that attackers used as an entry point had network access that extended to the POS environment. Furthermore, Target's FireEye security monitoring system had detected the malware and generated alerts, but the alerts were not acted upon because the procedures for alert triage and escalation were inadequate. The breach cost Target $292 million in total expenses. For CISM candidates, Target illustrates a principle that ISACA tests repeatedly: a policy without implementation, enforcement, and monitoring is not a control - it is a liability. The policy lifecycle must include verification that policies are actually implemented and operating effectively.

**Scenario 3 - SAMA Cybersecurity Framework Adoption (Regulatory Framework)**
In 2017, the Saudi Arabian Monetary Authority (SAMA) issued a mandatory Cybersecurity Framework for all financial institutions operating in the Kingdom. The framework draws from NIST CSF, ISO 27001, and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision's principles for operational resilience. It requires banks, insurance companies, and finance companies to implement controls across four domains: Cybersecurity Leadership and Governance, Cybersecurity Risk Management and Compliance, Cybersecurity Operations and Technology, and Third-Party Cybersecurity. Each institution must conduct an annual self-assessment and submit the results to SAMA. Independent auditors verify the assessment every two years. A major Saudi bank used this regulatory requirement as an opportunity to overhaul its entire security program, aligning its existing ISO 27001 ISMS with the SAMA-specific requirements and adding CIS Controls as tactical implementation guidance. The result was a layered framework approach that satisfied the regulator while providing actionable guidance for the security team.

**Scenario 4 - The Metric That Changed a Board's Mind (Program Metrics)**
A CISO at a European energy company struggled to secure budget for a security awareness program. The board viewed security training as a cost with no measurable return. The CISO implemented a pilot program and tracked a single metric: the phishing simulation click rate. Before the program, 28% of employees clicked on simulated phishing emails. After six months of monthly training and simulated campaigns, the rate dropped to 6%. The CISO then correlated this with actual incident data: phishing-related security incidents dropped by 71% during the same period, and the estimated cost avoidance (based on average incident response costs) was €340,000 - against a training program cost of €85,000. The board approved a full-scale rollout. The lesson: one well-chosen metric, tracked over time with clear business impact, is more persuasive than a dashboard of 50 technical indicators.

---

## Instructor Notes

**Common Misconceptions:**
- Students often ask "which framework is the best?" There is no single best framework. ISACA's position is that framework selection depends on organizational context - industry, size, regulatory environment, maturity level, and strategic objectives. The exam tests your ability to select and justify a framework, not to advocate for one over another.
- Many candidates confuse policies with procedures. On the CISM exam, this distinction matters. A question that asks about "management intent and direction" is asking about policy. A question about "step-by-step instructions" is asking about procedures. The correct answer depends on the level of the hierarchy being addressed.
- Students sometimes believe that metrics should always show improvement. In reality, a metric that reveals a problem is more valuable than one that hides it. The CISO who reports a rising phishing click rate is providing actionable intelligence; the one who reports only blocked attacks is providing comfort without insight.

**Exam Emphasis:**
- COBIT questions will test your understanding of its governance focus and design factors. Know that COBIT is ISACA's framework and that it bridges IT governance and information security governance.
- ISO 27001 questions will focus on the ISMS lifecycle (Plan-Do-Check-Act), the Statement of Applicability, and the certification process. You do not need to memorize all 93 Annex A controls, but you should understand the four themes (Organizational, People, Physical, Technological).
- Policy hierarchy questions are straightforward but common. Know the four levels (policy, standard, procedure, guideline) and who approves each level.
- Metrics questions test whether you understand the difference between operational and strategic metrics, and whether you can identify vanity metrics that do not drive decisions.

**Teaching Tips:**
- Use the Maersk case study as a powerful illustration of how frameworks provide structure for recovery, not just prevention. Students remember stories better than abstract concepts.
- For the framework comparison exercise, provide the three scenarios and have students debate in small groups. The discussion is more valuable than the "right" answer.
- The policy development exercise should use a realistic template. The SANS policy library is an excellent free resource that students can reference.
- For metrics, challenge students to identify vanity metrics in their own organizations. This generates lively discussion and practical insight.

---

## Discussion Questions

1. "Your organization has no formal security framework in place. The CEO asks you to recommend one. The company is a 300-person e-commerce retailer operating in the US and EU, subject to PCI DSS and GDPR. Which framework(s) would you recommend and in what order would you implement them?"

2. "You discover that your organization's security policies were last updated three years ago and do not address cloud computing, remote work, or AI tools. How would you prioritize the policy update process? Which policies would you address first?"

3. "A business unit leader complains that security policies are 'too restrictive' and prevent the team from working efficiently. The leader has been granting policy exceptions informally without going through the official exceptions process. How do you address this?"

4. "Your board asks for a 'single number' that represents the organization's overall security posture. Is this possible? What are the risks of oversimplifying security metrics, and how would you present a more nuanced view?"

---

## Hands-On Activity: Framework Selection & Policy Development

**Objective:** Students will select a framework for a fictional organization and draft the outline of an information security policy.

**Part 1 - Framework Selection:**

Three organizations need framework recommendations:

| Organization | Industry | Size | Regulatory Requirements | Current Maturity | Budget |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| AlphaFinance | Banking | 5,000 employees | SAMA, PCI DSS, GDPR | Low (Level 1) | High |
| BetaHealth | Healthcare | 200 employees | HIPAA, state privacy laws | Medium (Level 2) | Moderate |
| GammaStartup | SaaS Technology | 50 employees | SOC 2, GDPR | None | Low |

For each organization, students recommend: primary framework, supplementary framework(s), implementation timeline, and justification.

**Part 2 - Policy Outline:**

Students draft the outline of an Acceptable Use Policy for BetaHealth, including:
- Purpose and scope
- Key policy statements (at least 5)
- Roles and responsibilities
- Compliance and enforcement
- Exception process
- Review schedule

**Debrief:** Compare framework selections and policy outlines. Discuss how organizational context drives different choices. For GammaStartup, most students will recommend CIS Controls IG1 as a starting point with a path to SOC 2 - discuss why this is more practical than jumping straight to ISO 27001 certification.

---

## Session Summary

- **COBIT 2019** is ISACA's governance framework with 40 objectives across 5 domains and design factors for organizational tailoring. Expect it on the CISM exam as the bridge between IT governance and IS governance.
- **ISO/IEC 27001:2022** is the international ISMS standard with 93 Annex A controls. Certification provides external validation and is increasingly required by customers and regulators. Maersk's post-NotPetya rebuild demonstrates its value as a recovery and improvement framework.
- **NIST CSF 2.0** adds a Govern function to the original five, aligning with CISM's governance emphasis. Implementation tiers and profiles allow flexible adoption. Widely adopted globally, including as the basis for the SAMA Cybersecurity Framework.
- **CIS Controls v8** provides prioritized, actionable guidance through 18 control categories and three Implementation Groups. Ideal as a tactical complement to strategic frameworks.
- The **policy hierarchy** (policy → standard → procedure → guideline) creates a chain from management intent to operational execution. Each level has a different audience, approval authority, and update frequency.
- **Policy lifecycle management** ensures policies remain current, communicated, enforced, and effective. The Target breach illustrates the danger of policies that exist on paper but not in practice.
- **Security program metrics** must be meaningful, measurable, and actionable. Strategic metrics for the board, operational metrics for the security team. Avoid vanity metrics that look impressive but do not drive decisions.

---

## Preparation for Next Session

Session 8 moves from policy to practice - control design, selection, and implementation. We will explore how to translate policy requirements into operational controls, how to select controls based on risk assessment findings and framework guidance, and how to implement controls in a way that balances security effectiveness with business usability. Students should think about a security control they have implemented in their organization: what drove the decision? How was it selected? How was its effectiveness measured? These reflections will ground the next session in practical experience.

lectures.title: Day 8: Control Design, Selection & Implementation
lectures.content:
# Day 8 - Control Design, Selection & Implementation

## Module 3: Information Security Program | Session 8 of 14

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Exam Domain** | 3.0 - Information Security Program (33%) |
| **Objectives Covered** | Domain 3, Section B: Information Security Program Management (Part 1 - B.1, B.2) |
| **Delivery** | Live online (Zoom/Teams), bilingual English/Arabic |

---

## Session Overview

Policies declare intent. Controls deliver results. This session bridges the gap between what the security program says it will do and what it actually does. Control design, selection, and implementation represent the operational core of the information security program - the point where governance direction, risk assessment findings, and framework guidance converge into tangible, measurable security improvements.

We will examine the full lifecycle of a security control: from the initial design decision (what type of control is needed?) through selection (which specific control best addresses the risk?) to implementation (how do we deploy it without breaking the business?). Along the way, we will explore the taxonomy of controls - preventive, detective, corrective, compensating, deterrent, and directive - and how each type serves a different purpose in the defense-in-depth model.

The session draws heavily on real-world implementation experiences. We will study how Capital One's 2019 breach revealed a misconfigured web application firewall (WAF) - a control that was selected correctly but implemented incorrectly. We will examine how the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack in 2021 exposed the absence of basic controls (network segmentation, MFA on VPN) that would have prevented or contained the attack. These cases illustrate a principle that ISACA emphasizes throughout the CISM exam: a control that is poorly designed, incorrectly implemented, or inadequately maintained is not a control at all.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, students will be able to:

1. **Classify** security controls by function (preventive, detective, corrective, compensating, deterrent, directive) and by implementation type (administrative, technical, physical).
2. **Design** a defense-in-depth control architecture that provides layered protection across the technology stack.
3. **Select** appropriate controls based on risk assessment findings, framework guidance, regulatory requirements, and cost-benefit analysis.
4. **Implement** controls using a structured methodology that includes testing, change management, documentation, and user communication.
5. **Evaluate** control effectiveness through testing, monitoring, and metrics, identifying controls that are not operating as intended.
6. **Explain** the concept of compensating controls and when they are appropriate substitutes for primary controls.

---

## Exam Objectives Covered

| Objective | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **Domain 3, Section B** | Information Security Program Management |
| **B.1** | Information Security Control Design and Selection |
| **B.2** | Information Security Control Implementation and Integrations |

---

## Detailed Session Outline

| Topic | Activity Type | Details |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Session 7 Recap & Bridge** | Discussion | Review frameworks, policy hierarchy, and metrics. Bridge: frameworks tell us what controls to consider, policies tell us what is required, and risk assessment tells us where to focus. Now we design, select, and implement the controls that make it all real. |
| **Control Taxonomy: Function** | Lecture + Matrix | Six functional categories: (1) Preventive - stops incidents before they occur (firewall rules, access controls, encryption, security awareness training). (2) Detective - identifies incidents that have occurred or are in progress (IDS/IPS, SIEM alerts, audit logs, security cameras). (3) Corrective - restores systems to a known good state after an incident (backup restoration, patch deployment, incident response procedures). (4) Compensating - provides an alternative when the primary control is not feasible (e.g., enhanced monitoring when a system cannot support encryption). (5) Deterrent - discourages potential attackers or policy violators (login banners, security cameras, acceptable use policies). (6) Directive - mandates or guides behavior (policies, standards, procedures, training requirements). Build a matrix showing examples of each category across administrative, technical, and physical implementation types. |
| **Control Taxonomy: Implementation Type** | Lecture | Three implementation types: Administrative (policies, procedures, training, background checks, separation of duties). Technical (firewalls, encryption, access control lists, MFA, DLP, SIEM). Physical (locks, badges, security guards, environmental controls, CCTV). Emphasize that effective security requires all three types working together. A technical access control (MFA) is undermined if the administrative process (account provisioning) does not revoke access promptly when employees leave. Real-world example: the 2020 SolarWinds attack bypassed technical controls by compromising the software supply chain - an area where administrative controls (vendor risk management, code signing verification) were the primary defense. |
| **Defense-in-Depth Architecture** | Lecture + Diagram | Present the layered defense model: Data layer (encryption, DLP, rights management) → Application layer (secure coding, WAF, input validation) → Host layer (EDR, hardening, patch management) → Network layer (firewalls, segmentation, IDS/IPS) → Perimeter layer (DMZ, proxy, email gateway) → Physical layer (access controls, environmental) → Policy layer (governance, training, procedures). Walk through how an attack traverses these layers: a phishing email (perimeter) delivers malware (host), which moves laterally (network) to access a database (application/data). Each layer provides an opportunity to detect and stop the attack. If one layer fails, the next layer provides protection. |
| **Control Selection Process** | Lecture + Decision Framework | Structured approach to selecting controls: (1) Identify the risk to be addressed (from the risk register). (2) Determine the control objective (what must the control achieve?). (3) Identify candidate controls from framework guidance (ISO 27001 Annex A, CIS Controls, NIST SP 800-53). (4) Evaluate candidates against criteria: effectiveness (how well does it reduce risk?), cost (acquisition, implementation, maintenance), operational impact (does it impede business processes?), compatibility (does it integrate with existing systems?), and compliance (does it satisfy regulatory requirements?). (5) Select the optimal control or combination of controls. (6) Document the selection rationale. |
| **Case Study: Capital One Breach (2019)** | Case Study + Discussion | In July 2019, a former AWS employee exploited a misconfigured WAF to access Capital One's cloud-hosted data, exposing 106 million customer records including names, addresses, credit scores, and Social Security numbers. The WAF was the correct control selection - it should have prevented the attack. But the implementation was flawed: the WAF had been configured with an overly permissive IAM role that allowed it to access S3 buckets containing customer data. The attacker exploited a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability to assume the WAF's role and access the data. Lessons: (1) Control selection is necessary but not sufficient - implementation must be correct. (2) The principle of least privilege applies to service accounts and roles, not just human users. (3) Cloud security requires understanding the shared responsibility model - AWS secured the infrastructure, but Capital One was responsible for configuring its controls correctly. Capital One paid $80 million in regulatory fines and $190 million in a class-action settlement. |
| **Case Study: Colonial Pipeline (2021)** | Case Study + Discussion | In May 2021, the DarkSide ransomware group attacked Colonial Pipeline, which supplies 45% of the US East Coast's fuel. The attackers gained access through a compromised VPN account that used a reused password and did not require MFA. Once inside, the lack of network segmentation between the IT and OT (operational technology) networks allowed the ransomware to threaten pipeline operations. Colonial Pipeline paid a $4.4 million ransom (of which $2.3 million was later recovered by the FBI). Lessons: (1) Basic controls (MFA, network segmentation) would have prevented or contained the attack. (2) The absence of a control is itself a control failure - the risk assessment should have identified these gaps. (3) The business impact of a security failure can extend far beyond the organization - fuel shortages affected millions of people across the eastern United States. |
| **Compensating Controls** | Lecture + Examples | When the primary control is not feasible - due to technical limitations, cost, or business constraints - a compensating control provides an alternative. Requirements for a valid compensating control: it must address the same risk, provide a similar level of protection, and not introduce new risks. PCI DSS provides the most formal definition: a compensating control must meet the intent and rigor of the original requirement, provide a similar level of defense, be commensurate with the additional risk, and go above and beyond other PCI DSS requirements. Example: a legacy system cannot support TLS 1.2 encryption. Compensating controls: isolate the system on a dedicated network segment, implement enhanced monitoring and logging, restrict access to a limited number of authorized users, and schedule the system for replacement within 12 months. |
| **Control Implementation Methodology** | Lecture + Checklist | Structured implementation process: (1) Planning - define scope, timeline, resources, and success criteria. (2) Design - configure the control according to requirements and best practices. (3) Testing - verify the control works as intended in a test environment. Include both positive testing (does it block what it should?) and negative testing (does it allow what it should?). (4) Change management - follow the organization's change management process for production deployment. (5) Deployment - implement the control in production with rollback capability. (6) Validation - confirm the control is operating correctly in production. (7) Documentation - update the control inventory, procedures, and training materials. (8) Communication - inform affected users and stakeholders. (9) Monitoring - establish ongoing monitoring to verify continued effectiveness. |
| **Control Effectiveness Testing** | Lecture + Examples | Controls must be tested regularly to verify they are operating as intended. Testing methods: Vulnerability assessments (automated scanning for technical weaknesses). Penetration testing (simulated attacks to test control effectiveness). Tabletop exercises (scenario-based discussions to test procedures and decision-making). Red team exercises (adversarial simulations that test the entire defense-in-depth architecture). Audit reviews (systematic evaluation of control design and operating effectiveness). Continuous monitoring (automated, real-time verification of control status). Discuss the difference between control design effectiveness (is the control designed correctly?) and control operating effectiveness (is the control operating as designed?). |
| **Session Summary & Preview** | Wrap-up | Recap control taxonomy, defense-in-depth, selection process, implementation methodology, compensating controls, and effectiveness testing. Preview Session 9: Security Awareness, Training & Third-Party Management - the human and organizational dimensions of the security program. |

---

## Key Concepts & Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Preventive Control** | A security control designed to stop a security incident before it occurs. Examples: firewalls, access controls, encryption, security awareness training. |
| **Detective Control** | A security control designed to identify security incidents that have occurred or are in progress. Examples: IDS/IPS, SIEM, audit logs, security cameras. |
| **Corrective Control** | A security control designed to restore systems to a known good state after a security incident. Examples: backup restoration, patch deployment, incident response procedures. |
| **Compensating Control** | An alternative security control implemented when the primary control is not feasible, providing equivalent risk reduction. Must address the same risk and provide a similar level of protection. |
| **Defense-in-Depth** | A security strategy that employs multiple layers of controls across the technology stack, so that if one layer fails, subsequent layers continue to provide protection. |
| **Control Objective** | A statement of the desired result or purpose of implementing a particular control. Defines what the control must achieve, not how it achieves it. |
| **Shared Responsibility Model** | In cloud computing, the division of security responsibilities between the cloud service provider (infrastructure security) and the customer (configuration, data, and access management). |
| **SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)** | A vulnerability that allows an attacker to induce the server-side application to make HTTP requests to an arbitrary domain of the attacker's choosing, often used to access internal resources. |
| **Control Design Effectiveness** | An assessment of whether a control is designed correctly to achieve its objective. Evaluated through documentation review and design analysis. |
| **Control Operating Effectiveness** | An assessment of whether a control is operating as designed over a period of time. Evaluated through testing, monitoring, and audit. |

---

## Real-World Examples & Scenarios

**Scenario 1 - Defense-in-Depth at a Financial Institution (Control Architecture)**
A regional bank implements a defense-in-depth architecture to protect its online banking platform. Physical layer: data center with biometric access, CCTV, and environmental controls. Network layer: next-generation firewalls with application-layer inspection, network segmentation isolating the banking platform from the corporate network, and IDS/IPS monitoring all traffic. Host layer: hardened server configurations based on CIS benchmarks, EDR on all endpoints, and automated patch management. Application layer: secure coding practices verified by SAST/DAST, a WAF protecting the web application, and input validation on all user-facing forms. Data layer: AES-256 encryption for data at rest, TLS 1.3 for data in transit, and tokenization of credit card numbers. Policy layer: security awareness training for all employees, incident response procedures tested quarterly, and third-party penetration testing twice per year. When a phishing email bypasses the email gateway (perimeter failure), the EDR detects the malware on the endpoint (host layer success), quarantines the file, and alerts the SOC - demonstrating how layered controls contain threats even when individual layers fail.

**Scenario 2 - The SolarWinds Supply Chain Attack (Control Limitations)**
The SolarWinds attack, discovered in December 2020, compromised the Orion software update mechanism to distribute malware to approximately 18,000 organizations, including US government agencies and Fortune 500 companies. The attack bypassed traditional technical controls because the malware was delivered through a trusted software update channel - the very mechanism organizations rely on to maintain their security posture. This case illustrates the limits of technical controls and the importance of administrative controls in the supply chain: vendor risk assessments, code signing verification, software composition analysis, and the principle of zero trust (never trust, always verify - even trusted vendors). Organizations that had implemented network segmentation and least-privilege access were able to limit the blast radius of the compromise, even though they could not prevent the initial infection.

**Scenario 3 - PCI DSS Compensating Controls (Compensating Controls)**
A large hotel chain operates legacy property management systems that cannot be upgraded to support TLS 1.2 encryption. The systems process credit card transactions and are subject to PCI DSS requirements. Rather than accepting the risk or avoiding credit card processing entirely, the hotel chain implements compensating controls: (1) each legacy system is placed on an isolated network segment with no connectivity to the internet or other systems, (2) a modern payment terminal handles the actual card processing and communicates with the payment processor over TLS 1.3, (3) the legacy system receives only a tokenized reference - never the actual card number, (4) enhanced logging and monitoring track all access to the isolated segment, and (5) the hotel chain commits to replacing the legacy systems within 18 months. The PCI QSA (Qualified Security Assessor) reviews the compensating controls, verifies they meet the intent and rigor of the original requirement, and approves the approach. This is documented in the Compensating Controls Worksheet as part of the PCI DSS Report on Compliance.

---

## Instructor Notes

**Common Misconceptions:**
- Students often think of controls only in technical terms (firewalls, encryption, etc.). ISACA tests all three implementation types - administrative, technical, and physical. A question about "the most effective control for preventing unauthorized physical access" is asking about physical controls (badge readers, guards), not technical controls (access control lists).
- The distinction between preventive and detective controls is frequently tested. A firewall rule that blocks traffic is preventive. An IDS alert that notifies the SOC of suspicious traffic is detective. The same technology can serve different functions depending on configuration.
- Students sometimes assume that more controls equals better security. ISACA's position is that controls should be proportionate to risk. Over-controlling low-risk assets wastes resources and creates user friction that leads to workarounds - which may introduce new risks.

**Exam Emphasis:**
- Control classification questions are common: "Which type of control is [specific example]?" Know the six functional categories and three implementation types cold.
- Defense-in-depth questions test whether you understand the concept of layered protection and can identify which layer a specific control operates at.
- Compensating control questions will present a scenario where the primary control is not feasible and ask you to evaluate whether a proposed alternative is adequate. Apply the criteria: does it address the same risk? Does it provide similar protection? Does it introduce new risks?
- Implementation questions often focus on the change management and testing aspects. The correct answer usually includes testing before deployment and validation after deployment.

**Teaching Tips:**
- The Capital One and Colonial Pipeline case studies are powerful teaching tools. Use them to illustrate that control selection and implementation are separate challenges - both must be done correctly.
- For the defense-in-depth diagram, have students map their own organization's controls to the layers. This reveals gaps that they can address in their real-world roles.
- The control selection exercise should force trade-offs. Give students a limited budget and require them to prioritize - this teaches the cost-benefit analysis that ISACA expects.

---

## Discussion Questions

1. "The Capital One breach was caused by a misconfigured WAF, not a missing control. How does this change the way you think about control implementation? What processes should be in place to prevent configuration errors?"

2. "Your organization's legacy ERP system cannot support modern encryption standards. The system processes sensitive financial data. What compensating controls would you implement, and how would you document and justify them?"

3. "A colleague argues that investing in detective controls (SIEM, SOC) is more cost-effective than investing in preventive controls (firewalls, access controls) because 'you can never prevent everything.' Do you agree? How would you balance preventive and detective investments?"

4. "The Colonial Pipeline attack exploited the absence of MFA on a VPN account. MFA is a well-known, relatively inexpensive control. Why do organizations still fail to implement basic controls, and what can the information security manager do to address this?"

---

## Hands-On Activity: Control Selection & Design Workshop

**Objective:** Students will select and design controls for a fictional organization based on risk assessment findings.

**Scenario:**
MedTech Innovations is a medical device manufacturer with 800 employees. A recent risk assessment identified the following top risks:

| Risk ID | Risk Description | Risk Level | Current Controls |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| R-001 | Ransomware encrypts design files and production systems | Critical | Basic antivirus, weekly tape backups |
| R-002 | Insider threat: engineer steals proprietary device designs | High | Standard access controls, no DLP |
| R-003 | Supply chain attack through compromised firmware update | High | No firmware verification process |
| R-004 | Regulatory non-compliance with FDA cybersecurity requirements | High | Partial documentation, no formal program |
| R-005 | Cloud misconfiguration exposes patient data in test environment | Medium | Default cloud security settings |

**Student Task:**
For each risk, students must:
1. Identify the control objective (what must the control achieve?).
2. Select specific controls (at least 2 per risk, from different functional categories).
3. Classify each selected control (function + implementation type).
4. Estimate implementation complexity (Low/Medium/High).
5. Identify any compensating controls needed for constraints.
6. Prioritize the implementation order across all risks.

**Debrief:** Compare control selections and prioritization across groups. Discuss trade-offs: R-001 (ransomware) is critical but may require significant investment in EDR, network segmentation, and immutable backups. R-003 (supply chain) is high but may be addressed more quickly through administrative controls (firmware verification procedures). The prioritization discussion reveals different risk appetites and resource assumptions.

---

## Session Summary

- Security controls are classified by **function** (preventive, detective, corrective, compensating, deterrent, directive) and by **implementation type** (administrative, technical, physical). Effective security requires all types working together.
- **Defense-in-depth** provides layered protection across the technology stack. If one layer fails, subsequent layers continue to provide protection. The Capital One breach demonstrated that a correctly selected control (WAF) can fail if incorrectly implemented.
- **Control selection** follows a structured process: identify the risk, determine the control objective, evaluate candidate controls against effectiveness, cost, operational impact, compatibility, and compliance criteria, and document the rationale.
- The **Colonial Pipeline attack** illustrates that basic controls (MFA, network segmentation) remain the most impactful security investments. The absence of a control is itself a control failure.
- **Compensating controls** provide alternatives when primary controls are not feasible. They must address the same risk, provide similar protection, and not introduce new risks. PCI DSS provides the most formal framework for compensating control documentation.
- **Control implementation** requires a structured methodology: planning, design, testing, change management, deployment, validation, documentation, communication, and monitoring. Testing must include both positive and negative scenarios.
- **Control effectiveness testing** verifies that controls are operating as designed. Methods include vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, tabletop exercises, red team exercises, and continuous monitoring.

---

## Preparation for Next Session

Session 9 addresses the human and organizational dimensions of the security program: security awareness training, competency development, and third-party risk management. The human element remains the most exploited attack vector - Verizon's 2024 DBIR reports that 68% of breaches involve a human element. Students should reflect on their organization's security awareness program: is it effective? How do they know? What would they change? We will also examine how to manage the security risks introduced by third-party vendors, suppliers, and partners - a topic that has become critical in the era of supply chain attacks.

# Day 8 - Control Design, Selection & Implementation

## Module 3: Information Security Program | Session 8 of 14

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Exam Domain** | 3.0 - Information Security Program (33%) |
| **Objectives Covered** | Domain 3, Section B: Information Security Program Management (Part 1 - B.1, B.2) |
| **Delivery** | Live online (Zoom/Teams), bilingual English/Arabic |

---

## Session Overview

Policies declare intent. Controls deliver results. This session bridges the gap between what the security program says it will do and what it actually does. Control design, selection, and implementation represent the operational core of the information security program - the point where governance direction, risk assessment findings, and framework guidance converge into tangible, measurable security improvements.

We will examine the full lifecycle of a security control: from the initial design decision (what type of control is needed?) through selection (which specific control best addresses the risk?) to implementation (how do we deploy it without breaking the business?). Along the way, we will explore the taxonomy of controls - preventive, detective, corrective, compensating, deterrent, and directive - and how each type serves a different purpose in the defense-in-depth model.

The session draws heavily on real-world implementation experiences. We will study how Capital One's 2019 breach revealed a misconfigured web application firewall (WAF) - a control that was selected correctly but implemented incorrectly. We will examine how the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack in 2021 exposed the absence of basic controls (network segmentation, MFA on VPN) that would have prevented or contained the attack. These cases illustrate a principle that ISACA emphasizes throughout the CISM exam: a control that is poorly designed, incorrectly implemented, or inadequately maintained is not a control at all.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, students will be able to:

1. **Classify** security controls by function (preventive, detective, corrective, compensating, deterrent, directive) and by implementation type (administrative, technical, physical).
2. **Design** a defense-in-depth control architecture that provides layered protection across the technology stack.
3. **Select** appropriate controls based on risk assessment findings, framework guidance, regulatory requirements, and cost-benefit analysis.
4. **Implement** controls using a structured methodology that includes testing, change management, documentation, and user communication.
5. **Evaluate** control effectiveness through testing, monitoring, and metrics, identifying controls that are not operating as intended.
6. **Explain** the concept of compensating controls and when they are appropriate substitutes for primary controls.

---

## Exam Objectives Covered

| Objective | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **Domain 3, Section B** | Information Security Program Management |
| **B.1** | Information Security Control Design and Selection |
| **B.2** | Information Security Control Implementation and Integrations |

---

## Detailed Session Outline

| Topic | Activity Type | Details |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Session 7 Recap & Bridge** | Discussion | Review frameworks, policy hierarchy, and metrics. Bridge: frameworks tell us what controls to consider, policies tell us what is required, and risk assessment tells us where to focus. Now we design, select, and implement the controls that make it all real. |
| **Control Taxonomy: Function** | Lecture + Matrix | Six functional categories: (1) Preventive - stops incidents before they occur (firewall rules, access controls, encryption, security awareness training). (2) Detective - identifies incidents that have occurred or are in progress (IDS/IPS, SIEM alerts, audit logs, security cameras). (3) Corrective - restores systems to a known good state after an incident (backup restoration, patch deployment, incident response procedures). (4) Compensating - provides an alternative when the primary control is not feasible (e.g., enhanced monitoring when a system cannot support encryption). (5) Deterrent - discourages potential attackers or policy violators (login banners, security cameras, acceptable use policies). (6) Directive - mandates or guides behavior (policies, standards, procedures, training requirements). Build a matrix showing examples of each category across administrative, technical, and physical implementation types. |
| **Control Taxonomy: Implementation Type** | Lecture | Three implementation types: Administrative (policies, procedures, training, background checks, separation of duties). Technical (firewalls, encryption, access control lists, MFA, DLP, SIEM). Physical (locks, badges, security guards, environmental controls, CCTV). Emphasize that effective security requires all three types working together. A technical access control (MFA) is undermined if the administrative process (account provisioning) does not revoke access promptly when employees leave. Real-world example: the 2020 SolarWinds attack bypassed technical controls by compromising the software supply chain - an area where administrative controls (vendor risk management, code signing verification) were the primary defense. |
| **Defense-in-Depth Architecture** | Lecture + Diagram | Present the layered defense model: Data layer (encryption, DLP, rights management) → Application layer (secure coding, WAF, input validation) → Host layer (EDR, hardening, patch management) → Network layer (firewalls, segmentation, IDS/IPS) → Perimeter layer (DMZ, proxy, email gateway) → Physical layer (access controls, environmental) → Policy layer (governance, training, procedures). Walk through how an attack traverses these layers: a phishing email (perimeter) delivers malware (host), which moves laterally (network) to access a database (application/data). Each layer provides an opportunity to detect and stop the attack. If one layer fails, the next layer provides protection. |
| **Control Selection Process** | Lecture + Decision Framework | Structured approach to selecting controls: (1) Identify the risk to be addressed (from the risk register). (2) Determine the control objective (what must the control achieve?). (3) Identify candidate controls from framework guidance (ISO 27001 Annex A, CIS Controls, NIST SP 800-53). (4) Evaluate candidates against criteria: effectiveness (how well does it reduce risk?), cost (acquisition, implementation, maintenance), operational impact (does it impede business processes?), compatibility (does it integrate with existing systems?), and compliance (does it satisfy regulatory requirements?). (5) Select the optimal control or combination of controls. (6) Document the selection rationale. |
| **Case Study: Capital One Breach (2019)** | Case Study + Discussion | In July 2019, a former AWS employee exploited a misconfigured WAF to access Capital One's cloud-hosted data, exposing 106 million customer records including names, addresses, credit scores, and Social Security numbers. The WAF was the correct control selection - it should have prevented the attack. But the implementation was flawed: the WAF had been configured with an overly permissive IAM role that allowed it to access S3 buckets containing customer data. The attacker exploited a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability to assume the WAF's role and access the data. Lessons: (1) Control selection is necessary but not sufficient - implementation must be correct. (2) The principle of least privilege applies to service accounts and roles, not just human users. (3) Cloud security requires understanding the shared responsibility model - AWS secured the infrastructure, but Capital One was responsible for configuring its controls correctly. Capital One paid $80 million in regulatory fines and $190 million in a class-action settlement. |
| **Case Study: Colonial Pipeline (2021)** | Case Study + Discussion | In May 2021, the DarkSide ransomware group attacked Colonial Pipeline, which supplies 45% of the US East Coast's fuel. The attackers gained access through a compromised VPN account that used a reused password and did not require MFA. Once inside, the lack of network segmentation between the IT and OT (operational technology) networks allowed the ransomware to threaten pipeline operations. Colonial Pipeline paid a $4.4 million ransom (of which $2.3 million was later recovered by the FBI). Lessons: (1) Basic controls (MFA, network segmentation) would have prevented or contained the attack. (2) The absence of a control is itself a control failure - the risk assessment should have identified these gaps. (3) The business impact of a security failure can extend far beyond the organization - fuel shortages affected millions of people across the eastern United States. |
| **Compensating Controls** | Lecture + Examples | When the primary control is not feasible - due to technical limitations, cost, or business constraints - a compensating control provides an alternative. Requirements for a valid compensating control: it must address the same risk, provide a similar level of protection, and not introduce new risks. PCI DSS provides the most formal definition: a compensating control must meet the intent and rigor of the original requirement, provide a similar level of defense, be commensurate with the additional risk, and go above and beyond other PCI DSS requirements. Example: a legacy system cannot support TLS 1.2 encryption. Compensating controls: isolate the system on a dedicated network segment, implement enhanced monitoring and logging, restrict access to a limited number of authorized users, and schedule the system for replacement within 12 months. |
| **Control Implementation Methodology** | Lecture + Checklist | Structured implementation process: (1) Planning - define scope, timeline, resources, and success criteria. (2) Design - configure the control according to requirements and best practices. (3) Testing - verify the control works as intended in a test environment. Include both positive testing (does it block what it should?) and negative testing (does it allow what it should?). (4) Change management - follow the organization's change management process for production deployment. (5) Deployment - implement the control in production with rollback capability. (6) Validation - confirm the control is operating correctly in production. (7) Documentation - update the control inventory, procedures, and training materials. (8) Communication - inform affected users and stakeholders. (9) Monitoring - establish ongoing monitoring to verify continued effectiveness. |
| **Control Effectiveness Testing** | Lecture + Examples | Controls must be tested regularly to verify they are operating as intended. Testing methods: Vulnerability assessments (automated scanning for technical weaknesses). Penetration testing (simulated attacks to test control effectiveness). Tabletop exercises (scenario-based discussions to test procedures and decision-making). Red team exercises (adversarial simulations that test the entire defense-in-depth architecture). Audit reviews (systematic evaluation of control design and operating effectiveness). Continuous monitoring (automated, real-time verification of control status). Discuss the difference between control design effectiveness (is the control designed correctly?) and control operating effectiveness (is the control operating as designed?). |
| **Session Summary & Preview** | Wrap-up | Recap control taxonomy, defense-in-depth, selection process, implementation methodology, compensating controls, and effectiveness testing. Preview Session 9: Security Awareness, Training & Third-Party Management - the human and organizational dimensions of the security program. |

---

## Key Concepts & Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Preventive Control** | A security control designed to stop a security incident before it occurs. Examples: firewalls, access controls, encryption, security awareness training. |
| **Detective Control** | A security control designed to identify security incidents that have occurred or are in progress. Examples: IDS/IPS, SIEM, audit logs, security cameras. |
| **Corrective Control** | A security control designed to restore systems to a known good state after a security incident. Examples: backup restoration, patch deployment, incident response procedures. |
| **Compensating Control** | An alternative security control implemented when the primary control is not feasible, providing equivalent risk reduction. Must address the same risk and provide a similar level of protection. |
| **Defense-in-Depth** | A security strategy that employs multiple layers of controls across the technology stack, so that if one layer fails, subsequent layers continue to provide protection. |
| **Control Objective** | A statement of the desired result or purpose of implementing a particular control. Defines what the control must achieve, not how it achieves it. |
| **Shared Responsibility Model** | In cloud computing, the division of security responsibilities between the cloud service provider (infrastructure security) and the customer (configuration, data, and access management). |
| **SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)** | A vulnerability that allows an attacker to induce the server-side application to make HTTP requests to an arbitrary domain of the attacker's choosing, often used to access internal resources. |
| **Control Design Effectiveness** | An assessment of whether a control is designed correctly to achieve its objective. Evaluated through documentation review and design analysis. |
| **Control Operating Effectiveness** | An assessment of whether a control is operating as designed over a period of time. Evaluated through testing, monitoring, and audit. |

---

## Real-World Examples & Scenarios

**Scenario 1 - Defense-in-Depth at a Financial Institution (Control Architecture)**
A regional bank implements a defense-in-depth architecture to protect its online banking platform. Physical layer: data center with biometric access, CCTV, and environmental controls. Network layer: next-generation firewalls with application-layer inspection, network segmentation isolating the banking platform from the corporate network, and IDS/IPS monitoring all traffic. Host layer: hardened server configurations based on CIS benchmarks, EDR on all endpoints, and automated patch management. Application layer: secure coding practices verified by SAST/DAST, a WAF protecting the web application, and input validation on all user-facing forms. Data layer: AES-256 encryption for data at rest, TLS 1.3 for data in transit, and tokenization of credit card numbers. Policy layer: security awareness training for all employees, incident response procedures tested quarterly, and third-party penetration testing twice per year. When a phishing email bypasses the email gateway (perimeter failure), the EDR detects the malware on the endpoint (host layer success), quarantines the file, and alerts the SOC - demonstrating how layered controls contain threats even when individual layers fail.

**Scenario 2 - The SolarWinds Supply Chain Attack (Control Limitations)**
The SolarWinds attack, discovered in December 2020, compromised the Orion software update mechanism to distribute malware to approximately 18,000 organizations, including US government agencies and Fortune 500 companies. The attack bypassed traditional technical controls because the malware was delivered through a trusted software update channel - the very mechanism organizations rely on to maintain their security posture. This case illustrates the limits of technical controls and the importance of administrative controls in the supply chain: vendor risk assessments, code signing verification, software composition analysis, and the principle of zero trust (never trust, always verify - even trusted vendors). Organizations that had implemented network segmentation and least-privilege access were able to limit the blast radius of the compromise, even though they could not prevent the initial infection.

**Scenario 3 - PCI DSS Compensating Controls (Compensating Controls)**
A large hotel chain operates legacy property management systems that cannot be upgraded to support TLS 1.2 encryption. The systems process credit card transactions and are subject to PCI DSS requirements. Rather than accepting the risk or avoiding credit card processing entirely, the hotel chain implements compensating controls: (1) each legacy system is placed on an isolated network segment with no connectivity to the internet or other systems, (2) a modern payment terminal handles the actual card processing and communicates with the payment processor over TLS 1.3, (3) the legacy system receives only a tokenized reference - never the actual card number, (4) enhanced logging and monitoring track all access to the isolated segment, and (5) the hotel chain commits to replacing the legacy systems within 18 months. The PCI QSA (Qualified Security Assessor) reviews the compensating controls, verifies they meet the intent and rigor of the original requirement, and approves the approach. This is documented in the Compensating Controls Worksheet as part of the PCI DSS Report on Compliance.

# Day 9 - Security Awareness, Training & Third-Party Management

## Module 3: Information Security Program | Session 9 of 14

| | |
|:---|:---|
| **Exam Domain** | 3.0 - Information Security Program (33%) |
| **Objectives Covered** | Domain 3, Section B: Program Management (Part 2 - B.3, B.4, B.5) |
| **Delivery** | Live online (Zoom/Teams), bilingual English/Arabic |

---

## Session Overview

Technology does not click on phishing links. People do. Technology does not share passwords with colleagues. People do. Technology does not grant excessive access to third-party vendors because the procurement deadline is tomorrow. People do. This session addresses the two most persistent challenges in information security program management: transforming human behavior through awareness and training, and managing the security risks introduced by the organization's extended ecosystem of vendors, suppliers, and partners.

Verizon's 2024 Data Breach Investigations Report confirms what security professionals have known for decades: 68% of breaches involve a human element - whether through social engineering, errors, or misuse. No amount of technical controls can fully compensate for an untrained workforce. But traditional security awareness programs - annual compliance videos followed by a multiple-choice quiz - have proven largely ineffective. This session explores what actually works: behavioral science-informed approaches, continuous reinforcement, role-based training, and measurable outcomes.

The second half of the session tackles third-party risk management, a topic that has moved from a compliance footnote to a board-level concern. The SolarWinds attack (2020), the Kaseya VSA attack (2021), the MOVEit Transfer breach (2023), and the Change Healthcare attack (2024) have demonstrated that an organization's security is only as strong as its weakest vendor. We will examine the full lifecycle of third-party risk management: due diligence, contractual requirements, ongoing monitoring, and incident response coordination.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this session, students will be able to:

1. **Design** a security awareness and training program that uses behavioral science principles to drive measurable behavior change.
2. **Develop** role-based training curricula that address the specific risks and responsibilities of different organizational roles (executives, developers, finance, general staff).
3. **Measure** the effectiveness of security awareness programs using metrics that go beyond completion rates.
4. **Implement** a third-party risk management program that covers the full vendor lifecycle: due diligence, onboarding, ongoing monitoring, and offboarding.
5. **Evaluate** third-party security posture using questionnaires, audits, certifications, and continuous monitoring tools.
6. **Develop** contractual security requirements and SLAs for third-party engagements, including incident notification and right-to-audit clauses.

---

## Exam Objectives Covered

| Objective | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **Domain 3, Section B** | Information Security Program Management |
| **B.3** | Information Security Awareness and Training |
| **B.4** | Management of External Services (Third-Party Risk) |
| **B.5** | Information Security Program Communications |

---

## Detailed Session Outline

| Topic | Activity Type | Details |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Session 8 Recap & Bridge** | Discussion | Review control design, selection, and implementation. Bridge: controls are only as effective as the people who use them and the partners who connect to them. This session addresses the human and organizational dimensions that determine whether controls actually work in practice. |
| **The Human Element in Security Breaches** | Lecture + Statistics | Present data from Verizon's 2024 DBIR: 68% of breaches involve a human element. Social engineering accounts for 15% of breaches, with phishing remaining the top attack vector. Business Email Compromise (BEC) caused $2.9 billion in losses in 2023 according to the FBI's IC3 report. The median time for a user to click a phishing link is 21 seconds (Verizon DBIR 2024). These statistics establish the business case for investing in awareness and training - it is not a "nice to have" but a critical control. |
| **Why Traditional Awareness Programs Fail** | Lecture + Discussion | Annual compliance training fails because: (1) one-time exposure does not change behavior - the forgetting curve (Ebbinghaus) shows that people forget 70% of new information within 24 hours without reinforcement. (2) Generic content does not address role-specific risks - a developer faces different threats than a finance manager. (3) Passive learning (watching videos) does not build skills - active learning (simulations, exercises) is required. (4) Compliance-focused programs measure completion, not behavior change. Real-world example: Equifax's 2017 breach occurred despite the company having a security awareness program - the program did not effectively address the specific risk of unpatched vulnerabilities in the IT operations team. |
| **Behavioral Science-Informed Awareness** | Lecture | Apply behavioral science to security awareness: (1) Nudge theory - design the environment to make secure behavior the easy choice (e.g., password managers pre-installed, MFA enabled by default). (2) Social proof - share anonymized data showing that "87% of your colleagues completed the phishing simulation successfully." (3) Immediate feedback - when a user clicks a simulated phishing link, show the educational content immediately, not in a quarterly report. (4) Positive reinforcement - recognize and reward secure behavior rather than only punishing failures. (5) Spaced repetition - deliver short, frequent training modules (5 minutes monthly) rather than long annual sessions. Real-world example: KnowBe4's research shows that organizations using monthly phishing simulations with immediate feedback reduce click rates from an average of 34% to under 5% within 12 months. |
| **Role-Based Training Curricula** | Lecture + Matrix | Different roles face different risks and require different training. ---

## Key Concepts & Definitions

| Term | Definition |
|:---|:---|
| **Security Awareness Program** | A structured initiative designed to educate employees about information security risks, policies, and best practices, with the goal of changing behavior to reduce the organization's risk exposure. |
| **Phishing Simulation** | A controlled exercise in which simulated phishing emails are sent to employees to test their ability to recognize and report social engineering attempts. Results are used to measure awareness and target training. |
| **Role-Based Training** | Security training tailored to the specific risks, responsibilities, and technical requirements of different organizational roles, rather than generic one-size-fits-all content. |
| **Third-Party Risk Management (TPRM)** | The process of identifying, assessing, monitoring, and mitigating the security risks introduced by an organization's vendors, suppliers, partners, and other external parties. |
| **SIG (Standardized Information Gathering)** | A comprehensive vendor security assessment questionnaire developed by Shared Assessments, covering 18 risk domains including access control, network security, and incident management. |
| **CAIQ (Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire)** | A cloud-specific security assessment questionnaire developed by the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) for evaluating cloud service provider security controls. |
| **SOC 2 Type II** | An audit report that evaluates a service organization's controls over a period of time (typically 6–12 months) against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy. |
| **Security Rating Service** | A platform (e.g., BitSight, SecurityScorecard) that provides continuous, external assessment of an organization's security posture based on publicly observable data such as open ports, malware infections, and email security configuration. |
| **Fourth-Party Risk** | The security risk introduced by the subcontractors and service providers used by an organization's direct third-party vendors. Addressed through contractual flow-down requirements. |
| **Right-to-Audit Clause** | A contractual provision that grants the customer the right to conduct or commission security audits of the vendor's systems, processes, and controls. |

---

## Real-World Examples & Scenarios

**Scenario 1 - The MGM Resorts Social Engineering Attack (2023)**
In September 2023, the ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware group attacked MGM Resorts International, causing an estimated $100 million in losses. The attack began with a social engineering call to the MGM IT help desk. The attacker, posing as an employee, convinced the help desk to reset the employee's credentials - bypassing MFA. With valid credentials, the attackers moved laterally through the network, eventually deploying ransomware that shut down hotel check-in systems, slot machines, digital room keys, and the company's website for over a week. The attack exposed a critical gap in security awareness: the help desk staff were not trained to verify caller identity through a secondary channel before resetting credentials. A simple procedure - requiring the caller to verify their identity through a pre-registered callback number or in-person visit - would have prevented the initial compromise. MGM's competitor, Caesars Entertainment, was attacked by the same group using the same technique and paid a $15 million ransom. Both incidents underscore that security awareness must extend beyond phishing to include voice-based social engineering (vishing) and help desk procedures.

**Scenario 2 - The MOVEit Transfer Supply Chain Breach (2023)**
In May 2023, the Cl0p ransomware group exploited a zero-day SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2023-34362) in Progress Software's MOVEit Transfer file transfer application. The attack affected over 2,600 organizations and exposed the personal data of more than 77 million individuals. Victims included the BBC, British Airways, the US Department of Energy, Shell, Ernst & Young, and hundreds of other organizations that used MOVEit to transfer sensitive files. The breach highlighted several third-party risk management failures: many organizations did not know they were using MOVEit (it was deployed by their vendors or embedded in managed services), contractual incident notification requirements were inconsistent (some organizations learned about the breach from news reports rather than their vendors), and few organizations had assessed the security of their file transfer tools as part of their vendor risk management program. The MOVEit breach accelerated the adoption of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) requirements and continuous vendor monitoring services.

**Scenario 3 - The Change Healthcare Ransomware Attack (2024)**
In February 2024, the ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware group attacked Change Healthcare, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group that processes approximately 15 billion healthcare transactions annually - roughly one-third of all US healthcare claims. The attack disrupted pharmacy operations, claims processing, and payment systems across the entire US healthcare system for weeks. UnitedHealth Group reportedly paid a $22 million ransom. The attack exploited a Citrix remote access portal that did not have MFA enabled - the same basic control failure as Colonial Pipeline three years earlier. For third-party risk management, the Change Healthcare attack demonstrated concentration risk: when a single vendor processes such a large share of an industry's transactions, its failure becomes a systemic risk. Healthcare organizations that had identified Change Healthcare as a critical vendor and developed contingency plans recovered faster than those that had not assessed their dependency.
